utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you kindly call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. For the record, we have been informed that Mr. Nikolic, the accused, is not with us because of medical problems. Of course we wish him a quick return to the courtroom. In the meantime, I am also informed, please confirm, Madam Nikolic, that there is no concern on your part that we proceed in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no objections. We will know after the doctor's examination whether this will be just today or for the whole week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Madam Nikolic, and I'm sure you will come back to us. Mr. Sarapa is back, Mr. Bourgon is not here as explained by Ms. Nikolic. The rest of the teams are here. And the Prosecution, apart from Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls and also Ms. Soljan -- I find it difficult to pronounce your name. Soljan. Okay. I notice that the witness is not in. Are there any preliminaries that would you like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good afternoon. I just have a scheduling matter I would like to bring up with the Court and perhaps I'm looking at this a bit negatively, but the good news is that we're going much quicker and we expect to keep that pace. The bad news is that we had planned for this week to, in addition to this witness, have three more witnesses, and if -- but if we keep this pace and in talking to the counsel, we don't see that they have a whole lot of cross-examination, we could very well finish early on Friday and have time left. I may be wrong, I have that worry every Wednesday and most -- and I have not had that problem yet, but it looks like with your new schedule, we may have some time. I've tried to bring in other people, but given visa issues and other things, I'm told it can't be done. We're trying but it looks like we may have some time. I've been wrong in the past, but we're going -- the train is a little ahead of us, we will catch up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose in that case, we can start doing some brainstorming to identify some legal issue pending between the two of you, which we could deal with on Friday if we finish early with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I've asked Defence counsel, they've referred me to Mr. Bourgon, and we can see if there's something we can argue about, but also there is a video or two that we might play, but we're looking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is fine. And also perhaps I think it's high time now we bring the Ruez and images matter to an end. There has been ample time for the Defence to consult with you, enabling you to go back to the American Embassy and conclude the matter. So perhaps we could do that on Friday. Judge Kwon? Yeah. So it's an invitation to the Defence teams to try thinking about a possible debate on this matter on Friday or some other matter, issue that you wish to debate. All right? I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Are there any other preliminary matters you would like to raise? I hear none. Can we draw down the curtains, please, and bring in the witness, Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir. We're going to proceed with the cross-examination and hopefully finish within a short time. Mr. Lazarevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We will continue where we left off yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear what the counsel is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, it could be the curtains, but the interpreters couldn't follow, couldn't hear what you were saying. So if you can -- let's finish until the curtains are up and then proceed with repeating your question, please. And you need -- okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, it wasn't quite a question, I just said to the witness that we shall continue where we stopped yesterday. Nothing more than that. Now, can we have on the e-court, document number 993D. Can we go a bit lower? That's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I assume that Mr. Nicholls showed you this document when you were preparing to testify. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, of course you can remember, if when you were noting down this intercept that we see in front of us, if you changed your pen at some point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, it's understandable after so many years. But let us look at the original document and let's try to clarify some things just so that it's clear in the transcript what is actually written there. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... I would kindly ask them to give to Madam Usher notebook number 232, and it's page number 01077793, I believe it's already marked with a blue marker. Pull it a bit up, just to make sure that this -- that's it. Thank you very much. And just a bit down, because I want to discuss the whole -- that's it. Thank you. [Interpretation] Witness, you see for yourself the original of the notebook. So if we can just clarify some things that we can see now that we're looking at the original. Before that we were looking at a copy. Let's start from what is written at the top. What's written at the top is (redacted) can you see that? If I'm not mistaken that is not your handwriting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And this is written with a pencil if you can see it there. Can 4 you tell us what this word (redacted) means and who wrote that. With just one warning, if it's some colleague of yours that you worked with together, please tell us right away so that we can move into private session so we don't identify him in open session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prefer that we go into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we go --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay, yes. Thank you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, when we look, we see that it says 785000, then we have 5 or 3 CH then 20 or 21:40. We can see that certain corrections were made here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me now whether what was written in black pen was written first or whether what is written in red was written first? Because then we could work out what was corrected of the two.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing that was written was written in red pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And if you can also tell me here in front of this CH, was it 5 and changed to 3? Is that the correction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was 3 and that it -- later it was changed to a 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you explain the same thing for the time? I think it's this part that comes after that, what was the original and what was the correction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original was written in red, and the correction was written in the dark ink.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me when the correction was made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I explain what this is about in this particular case? It's like this: There was a conversation which was written in red ink, the information regarding that conversation was written in red. Then it was decided that the conversation was not important, so the red writing remained. When a new conversation came up, I just left the information in red and I just corrected the information that pertained to this later conversation, and then I continued to note it down after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that is a satisfactory explanation. I would like to ask you, would this frequency 785000 and this 5 or 3, the indication of the channel, it doesn't matter what it is, were you able, on the basis of these two pieces of information, to conclude where the collocutor marked as Y was actually located during this conversation? Can this be concluded on the basis of this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When you were testifying yesterday at one point Mr. Nicholls asked you why X and Y were used and then after that General Krstic, Borovcanin from special forces, and now I would like to be quite specific so this can go in the transcript. This is on page 5928 of yesterday's transcript. [In English] "In this intercept in line two, it states: 'Hello, this is Borovcanin. General, how are you?' And at the top you have written 'Borovcanin from the specials.' Can you tell us why you wrote that 'from the specials' after Borovcanin's name at the top?" [Interpretation] That was the question from the Prosecution and your answer was as follows: "[In English] That was on the device. I heard him introduce himself. But that part had not been recorded. That is why it is not in the transcribed portion." [Interpretation] Does this help? You have read your answer back to you what you told the Prosecutor to his question yesterday. If I understand your answer correctly, you stated an assumption why something was written, and not that you actually remember why this was written.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case I don't recall, but I could explain in principle what the procedure was, how I actually did the job and perhaps then it would be clear to you. Would you like me to explain it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, we do have your testimony from the Krstic case. We have the transcript. So we are more or less familiar with that, but we are interested in this specific case if you remember this being so specifically, or you just assumed that that's how it was and we are interested in the question by the Prosecutor from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from this late distance, it's been a long time since then, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. So on the basis of your answer I conclude that it is your assumption that you heard that Borovcanin was from the specials before the conversation was taped and that's why you wrote it down. You wrote it down based on what you remembered at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably I heard when he was calling the switchboard operator, I heard him introduced himself like that and I started to record and at that time, most probably, I wrote this down so that I wouldn't forgot it later. And the actual text was transcribed later, after the text was heard back, after the tape recording was listened to and then the conversation was transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the 92 summary is the witness's ICTY statement because my friend said we've got your Krstic testimony, so I just -- in case there was any misunderstanding on his part, it's not the Krstic testimony that we're submitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic, I think he's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, but I wanted to make use a little bit more on Krstic transcript. This is why I said that it was already testified here about. Well, maybe because at this point I'm going to quote some parts from Krstic case, so maybe we should move into private session as that was the case before when Madam Fauveau did so as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's revert to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have just read the question and your answer to the question in the Krstic case. And, as you have heard after I testified -- actually, after I presented to you, you probably, after listening back to the tape, understood that it was Borovcanin from the specials. Was that your assumption at the time also when you testified about it in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I am not going to misunderstand. If you don't answer it, I mean it's been a long time since then, so it's clear that this is an assumption of yours about what you wrote down at the time rather than a clear recollection of why you happened to write that down. I mean do you - - do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you in principle, but if possible I would like to just explain one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always took care that the information that I jotted down would be as accurate as possible. I didn't want to risk ever - I remember that very well - risk sending the wrong information to the higher command. I would rather not send any information than send the wrong information to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And of course you carried out your duties as best you knew how. However, since we are talking about assumptions here, if I were to tell you that a colleague of yours who was here could also say something along the lines of yes, he's the one from the specials, could that have been another way of finding out what this entry is about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such cases, there should have been a question mark next to the information, and I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us have a look at the conversation and its continuation. I think you saw it during proofing as well. It carries on to the next page. Can we conclude that there is no name there, no mention of names apart from Borovcanin and Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If we go back to the beginning we see that it starts with, "Hello, this is Krstic." And the answer is, "Hello, this is Borovcanin. General, how are you?" You will agree with me this hello is a usual greeting when beginning a telephone link or radio link.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is symptomatic of a telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that this marks the beginning of the conversation, they introduced themselves to each other, they said hello?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If we go down the page, if we look at the conversation itself, and not the mentioning of the participants in the heading, in the very text of the conversation we don't see the word "special" or "specials" anywhere, do we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us put aside the fact that it says "Borovcanin from the specials" at the top. Let us look at the text only, the text of the conversation as it stands. And we are now interested in the last name, Borovcanin. [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] It seems we have some problem with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You can tell me what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was asking for a private session just very briefly. And I don't see -- see this recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If Mr. Lazarevic switches from B/C/S into English without pause, then what happens is an overlap between the interpreter and what he is actually saying in English, therefore the court reporter cannot take down both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that's what I'm sure happened. So shall we continue? Yeah, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, to be honest, I would invite Mr. Lazarevic to repeat what he has just stated so it is on record in open session, and then Mr. McCloskey can address it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'll do it. Well, at this moment I would like the Prosecution to stipulate that they are not in possession of the audio recording of the above-mentioned conversation and they never had it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can simply say, yes, we don't have such an audio recording; however, I would object to this as a method to question the Prosecution mid-witness regarding stipulations. I welcome stipulations, I would prefer them discussed outside of court so we can properly prepare. There are a lot of intercepts, that would be a lot of questions to ask the Prosecution. So there is no audio of this, but if we could find a better way of getting at it, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still no harm done, so I think we can proceed. Have you finished with the witness, or not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By all means, that was my last question. I could have asked the witness if he was aware of such a tape, but it was simpler to do it with our colleagues. So I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So there is still Mr. Meek and Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we have no question of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. And Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. President, nor do I. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That basically means we have concluded with this witness, unless there is a re-examination or any questions on our part. Mr. Nicholls, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could have one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, while you were being questioned by my colleague just now, you said you wanted to explain more, and I think it was why you wrote down "from the specials," and your explanation would have been according to your practice, you could explain why that might be there. You said that you would try to be as accurate as possible in any information you sent. If you have anything more to explain about why you wrote that down "from the specials," I think I would like to give you the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-134 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thing I wrote down, well, I can't recall exactly, but I still remember the way I noted things down. Next to this piece of information, there is no question mark which means that I was certain that the information was true. And another thing, as for military communications, only a limited number of soldiers has the right of access. Therefore, if there are say a dozen Borovcanins in a unit, it is most likely that only one has access to communication, whereas the rest do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Judge Kwon, do you have any questions? Judge Prost, Judge Stole? Witness, that brings your testimony to an end here. I wish to thank you for coming over to give evidence, and our staff will assist you to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home. Now, the next witness enjoys pseudonym and facial distortion only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, we can start dealing with the tendering process. Defence teams have received a copy of the list of documents that the Prosecution is seeking to tender. Is there any objection? Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Basically I have the same objection as yesterday. It refers to the audiotape, as mentioned in the documentation forwarded by the Prosecutor under the number 1387D. I do not wish to repeat my reasons, as I've stated those yesterday. Referring to the previous witness. The same stands forces this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic, and that will be dealt with the same way we dealt with it yesterday. If the Prosecution insists in tendering it, because you didn't make use of it with this witness, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do tender it, Your Honour. To save time I didn't play it, but what I had him do was confirm that it had been played and that it was his intercept and it was the same one he had recorded in the exhibit. And my response, I will rely on Mr. Thayer's representations to the same issue yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That can be dealt with easily, with relative ease. Any further objections? So the first two of these documents, 2356 and 2357 will be admitted and remain under seal and the rest is marked for identifications purposes only with the understanding that the bold, the ones in bold characters will be kept under seal until finally determined. Then I think there are some Defence teams that wish to tender some documents. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have attached it. We forwarded a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't let me finish. I have two of you. That's Madam Fauveau and yourself. Again, they are on lists that have been submitted. In the case of the documents tendered by Madam Fauveau, translation is still pending, so they will be marked for identification. I take it there is no objection on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Although I think one of the Popovic exhibits for submissions have already been submitted. It's same one, but it's...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Zivanovic agrees to that. There is no need. The other two remaining would be 1D93, which will be marked for identification purposes only, pending translation. And 1D156, and I hear no objection, so that is admitted. All right. Can we move to the next witness? Now, as regards this next witness, the regime that we put in place the day before yesterday will be in force. All right. I think you were right in your assessment, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And may I be excused for one minute? I will be back, but don't wait for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you were right in your assessment, let us hope it doesn't create us a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can start [microphone not activated]. Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I welcome you to this Tribunal. You are soon going to start giving evidence. I think you will feel very warm in that jacket in here. Our rules require that before you start giving evidence you undertake to speak the truth. So Madam Usher is going to give you the text of the solemn declaration you are required to enter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. I could kindly take a seat, make yourself comfortable. Ms. Soljan, who I understand you have already met, will be examining you in chief by reference to your witness statement of the 12th May 1999. And then she will follow with a few questions, after which there will be some cross-examinations from the Defence teams. Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. If I could please have the usher's providing the witness with what has been marked for identification as PO2360. Witness, if you would please take a look at the piece of paper, without reading the name out loud, please confirm that that is indeed your name? You can just answer by saying "yes" if it is indeed?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That will go under seal and if you could just -- thank you. Show it to our colleagues. Thank you very much. Now, sir, do you recall providing information to the Office of the Prosecutor in May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, I provided a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you read your statement in my office a few days ago; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that the statement is correct and accurate, that the information in the statement is correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions again, would you answer in the same way?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I will read a short summary of that statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Soljan, before you do so. For the record, this witness will be referred to as PW-134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Here I have it 134. 135, yes, correct. And in addition, sir, you know that you have been also granted face distortion, apart from the use of a pseudonym, as per the 16th November decision of the Trial Chamber. So go ahead, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will proceed to now read the short summary of the statement of May 1999. The witness is a Bosnian Muslim who was bone in Tuzla in 1973. He performed his mandatory service with the JNA in 1991 and 1992 during which time he was attached to a signals unit and learned how to use various types of communications equipment. Now, Your Honours, if I could please go into private session for the reading of the second paragraph since it contains sensitive information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: The witness's work practice followed the established procedure of scanning, recording and transcribing intercepts into notebooks. Normal practice was to work in six-hour shifts followed by a six-hour break, depending on how busy it was. During the fall of Srebrenica in 1995, everyone was working continuously. Over time, the operators grew to know which channels were worth monitoring on particular frequencies and became skilled at identifying the voices of many of the monitored individuals. The witness himself was able to recognise several voices of VRS officers and code names. That ends the summary of the statement which, for the record, is PO2359.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the last few days did you review seven handwritten copies of intercepts in a tabbed blue binder?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you identify all seven of those as your original handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you also review those same intercepts in their original notebooks?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... also confirm that they were your original handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And can you confirm, as you sit here before the Trial Chamber today, that you have listened to, recorded and transcribed these seven intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Other than the handwritten intercepts, did you also have the opportunity to take a look at the typed versions of these intercepts?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And in your review of the intercepts of the handwritten intercepts and the typed version, did you notice that sometimes there were differences between the notebook version and the typed version?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I would like to go to one such intercept and ask you a couple of questions about it. If we could please turn to 65 ter number 1122B and C. The B/C/S handwritten as well as typed-up version. If it's possible to show those on the same screen, that will ideal. If not, we can go from one to the other. This is also the version that has been provided to the Defence under tab 2. Now, sir, do you recognise this intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... intercept?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And for the record, on -- right where we begin where we start where it says 259.675, U, 18, and what appears to be 48. Could we for a moment get version C of this very same intercept, please. Blown up a little bit, please, and I believe it will actually begin at ERN 0320-5261, page 2. If we could just scroll towards the bottom of page 2. At the bottom of that page, if we could just focus in on the intercept that also begins with the numbers 259. Right. 259.675. Where the time is 1855. Can you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us -- as we can all see, there is a difference -- the frequency number appears to be the same. But there is a difference between the hour, the hour determination in between the two, one says -- the typed version says 1855, the handwritten version says 1848. Could you explain for us, please, how that could be?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I can. It's easy. Possibly there was a mistake when that intercept was being typed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, let's take a further look at this intercept, please. When we look at the line below the time, in the handwritten intercept there is a line which says -- well, in this version here we may need to put it up -- put the handwritten version on the ELMO for a little period of time because it seems to be a little cut off, but it says "Rajko - Panorama - Panorama 3." Now, below that is the first, the beginning of the conversation, and the very first line of the conversation in the typed intercept begins with an X, identifies the speaker with an X. In your handwriting version of the intercept, it identifies the first speaker as 03. Could you explain that for us, sir? Is there -- is that a significant difference?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No. Both participants started with the same name, so during the typing you would put the first letter or the initial, and so that the encryption person could differentiate between them, he marked one as X and the other one as panorama, the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So would it, in fact, be correct to say that what is in the handwritten version identified as 03, is indeed equivalent to what is in the typed version identified as X?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And one more question. Now, if we can just focus on the speaker identification on the first six lines of the handwritten version. In the handwriting version, the first line is being spoken by 03, second line is spoken by C, third line is spoken by 03, fourth line is spoken by R. Fifth line is spoken by 03 again, and the sixth line is spoken by R. So the rest of the conversation then continues between R and 03. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, if we take a look at the typed version, the order is -- first line X, second line the speaker is C, third line the speaker is X, fourth line the speaker is C, fifth line the speaker is R, and sixth line the speaker is X and again it continues between R and X. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, there appears to be a difference that begins as of line 4 between these two intercepts, the versions of the intercept. Could you explain for the -- to the Trial Chamber what the difference is?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: The difference is in line 4, it's a mistake. The starting initials were mixed up from line 4 until the end of the conversation, so it is a mistake in the transcription of the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So you're saying the mistake began in the -- was -- took place in the handwritten version of the intercept; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that in the handwriting it is indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object. Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Object to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question. It is a question of knowing whether the mistake was made in the handwritten version. The Prosecution is suggesting that the mistake was made in the handwritten version. I object to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps you can rephrase the question, although it has been answered already, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, the witness just began explaining this, and so I will indeed continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, you had just mentioned, Witness, that in the handwritten version it is indicated. Can you show to us what indeed is indicated in the handwritten version? What happened?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: In line 4, the beginning of line 4 is underlined, and from there onwards the initials R and 03 were mixed. They were substituted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And could you indicate for the Court more precisely where exactly is this line?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: "Hey, that's you, Rajko Vlah here." From that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Underneath the line that says [B/C/S spoken]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, from that line. From that line [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Perhaps for easier viewing, it's been a little bit cut off in the photocopied version. If we could place it on the ELMO so that this line can be indicated more clearly. Now, sir, can you maybe indicate, point with a pen where this line is?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you drew this line, sir? You had drawn this line; is that correct? Don't -- yeah. At the time in 1995, when you -- when you took down this intercept, did you write this line?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, after transcribing the conversation, I concluded that there was a mistake and so I told that the person who was retyping the conversation and we made the correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Soljan. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. I saw you standing up. I presumed -- I assumed that you wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought that we were now going to begin the cross-examination, so that's why I stood up. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That's what we are going to do. What surprised me is seeing you standing up, because the information that we received at the beginning before this witness started to give evidence was to the effect that only D4 and D5 would be cross-examining the witness. You wish to cross-examine the witness as well? Go ahead. By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Witness, we received information about your conversation with the Prosecution before you came to testify, or some days before you came to testify. Yesterday or the day before. You remember that, I'm sure, that you talked with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will remind you that in that conversation, amongst other things, you said that the information about the direction of the conversation and the azimuth were not noted down in the notebook because the person who was typing it into the computer could conclude that on the basis of the frequency and the channel; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you had your own personal notebook where you noted information about the frequencies and the persons you were surveilling, and then this notebook was destroyed after the war; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. The notebook was destroyed in 1995 or 1996, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain -- well, you also said that it was the practice of many operators to have these personal notebooks, that they had them also?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: We can call them notebooks, but they were just personal notes. You couldn't remember everything without them, so you just had these notes with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So these were not proper notebooks, they were just note pads, something like that?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what the difference was between the note pads and the notebooks that you received from the command?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: The notebooks that came from the command were used only to transcribe intercepts while these private notebooks, note pads, mine, for example, contained all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, when you say "all sorts of things," I assume that they're personal and private notes of yours, but from what I was able to see from this information from the Prosecutor, this private note pad or notebook of yours also contained information about frequencies and the persons that you were monitoring; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why this official information was entered into this personal notebook or note pad?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Well, there were many names, many frequencies, many things, and you would forget them in time. But after a certain amount of time, it was very useful. You would use it again. So we would use that to just recollect -- refresh or recollection to see what was what.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever put information from your personal notebooks into the official notebook?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that at the location where you worked, and I'm not going to mention the name, that there was just one person in charge of entering the information into a computer, and in order to help him operators frequently entered their own text into the computer. Was that how it was?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also do that?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: In some cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you did that at the time, did you also encrypt this text that you had typed into the computer?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The text that you typed into the computer and sent, did you also send it?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No, I was just helping my colleague by typing the text, but the encryption and sending off of the text was something that the colleague did. We were not authorised to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard my learned friend, the Prosecutor, reading that in the fall -- during the fall of Srebrenica, all of you worked constantly; in other words, there was more work than usual. You were under more pressure than usual.

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We worked for 20 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean daily shifts, during the course of the day, you all worked for 20 hours?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, from the early morning hours until late at night sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me how many devices or workstations you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I will be able to give you a correct answer. I think there were two or three multi-channel combinations, and also the same for single-channel devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You will remember that the first time you had contacts with the Tribunal was through an investigator when you gave a statement. This was sometime -- actually, this was on the 6th and the 12th of May, 1999. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you said that sometimes you didn't have enough notebooks and that you had to write down the conversations in the same format as you did in the notebooks, but on a piece of paper. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes. They were just sheets of paper which were already used on one side and then we would use the back of the sheet of paper, which was clean, to write down on -- there was a shortage of paper at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The things that you noted down on those sheets of paper, when you didn't have notebooks, did you enter the information from those sheets of paper into your personal notebook?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No. We did not, because we didn't have these books then. I mean if we had them, we wouldn't have had to use the sheets of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't even have this note pad that we talked about before, this personal notebook, this is what I was thinking of?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did have that. But it's a small diary, it's a small pad, so I wouldn't be able to put all of that in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Later, did you enter that into the notebook that you received from the command, once you received it from the command?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: You mean did we transfer the information from the sheets of paper into this official notebook or from my personal notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Meaning the sheets of paper -- the information from the sheets of paper, was that entered into the notebooks once you get them -- once you got them?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No, this was later just clipped together, and it was probably kept in some archive, I actually don't know where these sheets of paper were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have one more question. Do you remember how many notebooks were used at the same time, I'm talking about from the command now, I'm not talking about these personal notebooks of yours.

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: There was the same number of notebooks as workstations, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said earlier -- and you mentioned that you mean two or three, these combinations?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes. Each workstation was supposed to have a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this notebook - actually, you received a fresh notebook only once the -- ones you were using were completely full; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Just to make sure now, we will try to update this list. Beara Defence, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Borovcanin team, you have 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If this is agreeable to you, Mr. Stojanovic, rather than starting now and stopping in five minutes' time for the break and then resuming, I suggest we take the break straight away now and we need 25 minutes now, no? 25 minutes, and then you start immediately after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness, I'm going to put some questions to you relating to one intercept. Could we please look at Exhibit PO1140P in the e-court system in the B/C/S version and then we also would like to use PO1140A and we would need that document in the English version. Otherwise, Your Honours, on the 65 ter list it's Prosecution number 1140, and it's in tab 6. Thank you. Sir, do you see in front of you to the right an intercept in handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the time that you marked and the date that we have, and that's from before, and we know that it's the 13th of July at 1530 hours, could you please help us and tell us, in view of the channel and the frequency that you were monitoring, can you please tell us where the X and Y speakers are located or approximately where they are located?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please help us and read this word that you wrote down in the area of, and then it's a word that is perhaps a geographical name or a toponym or something?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I think the word is Uducac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the -- of Mount Udric, and is it something that is familiar to you in view of the area you come from?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Mount Udric is in eastern Bosnia, to the south of the town of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I think that is so, but I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that in listening to this intercept instead of the Udric sector, you heard and wrote down the word sector Uducac?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: What is written here, I think, is supposed to be the way it is written, otherwise I would have marked it with a question mark or dots or something, or I would simply call my colleagues and we would listen back to it together, so I do believe that this is how it is supposed to be written.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And have you ever heard of Uducac as a toponym or a geographical name?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, I would like to ask you the following: In view of the fact that you said that there were sometimes differences between the handwritten text and the typed text that was sent for crypto-protection, if there are differences which of those two texts, according to you, is more authentic and more accurate?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Well, the one -- the authentic one that has been -- that is the transcription of the recording is more accurate. It's more accurate than the typewritten text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Which one would be sent to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: The typewritten text would be sent to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, is it fair to say when started working in the unit in the northern location, you worked first on jamming and scrambling telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: In the beginning I worked as a scrambler, but not of telephone conversations, but of tactical connections.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you stopped working as a scrambler, did the other members in your unit carry on this work of scrambling or jamming telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because -- we need to clear this. In spite of the witness's previous answer, namely that he was not referring to scrambling telephone conversations but tactical communications, connections, your subsequent question referred to telephone conversations. And he has now also answered in relation to telephone conversations. I think we need to have it clear whether we are talking of telephone conversations or other sorts of conversations that were being scrambled. I leave it in your hands, Madam Fauveau, I just wanted to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there must have been a mistake in the translation. I talked about tactical conversations that the witness mentioned. I worked scrambling -- I talked about scrambling in general. It might be in our best interests to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when you stopped working as a scrambler of tactical conversations, did anybody carry on with that work after you?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, the unit continued to be in existence, but I was not part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In your statement you made for the Prosecution in 1999, you said that you reused the tapes when they were full. When you reused the tapes, did the conversations recorded on the tape, were they erased or did you rerecord on the tapes you had rewound?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: When we were short of tapes, we would rerecord them. If there was an order from the command to leave a particular intercept on the tape, that would be left and sent to the archives. Everything else would be recorded over.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And when the tapes were reused and new conversations were recorded over the previous conversations, could it happen that the recording was not perfect and that the two conversations would overlap; the older one and the more recent one?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No, it couldn't happen. There is, however, a possibility that after multiple use the recording wouldn't be of the same quality, but the old recording would always be erased and there was no possibility of the two overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said earlier on that sometimes you would type in the conversations in the computer, but somebody else would encrypt them and send them. When you typed in a conversation on the computer, would you put your initials below this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Usually I would put my initials there, but it wasn't a practice. The only thing that was important to note down was to mark the spot to which a particular conversation had been transcribed, to put it in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to see Exhibit P1122, P1122B, and P1122C. The English version would be A and D.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, just before, in this conversation there is mention made of panorama. Would it be correct to say that this was a coded name of a unit of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, it was their code-name.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know whether the army of Republika Srpska would often change these coded names?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I think some code names were around for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And as for this particular name, Panorama, do you know when you heard it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I cannot recall an exact time, since in certain situations -- well, say you receive an order to monitor another direction, another channel, and then there is a month or two that you haven't used a particular frequency and you don't hear the same code-names and then you go back to the old names. Therefore, I really cannot say when I heard of that name for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know by any chance in what year that might have been? Was it 1994, 1995, or even 1993?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, when we look at this conversation, it's Exhibit 1122D, could we show the second page? Excuse me, it's probably my mistake. It was 1122C. And the second page, please. Sir, when one looks at these two conversations on the first line, the first line reads, "Is the big boss there?" It appears that this was uttered by Panorama 03. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And then further on on the second line, there is one person on the typewritten version, which is named the C speaker, could you tell us who this might be? I'm not asking you to tell their name, but do you know who this might have been, what this person's responsibility was and why this person was mentioned as C?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I think it was the switchboard's name, the operator's.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this operator, unlike Panorama 03, would have been the Panorama speaker?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does this seem logical to you that Panorama 03, which was probably located in Panorama, would call Panorama?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: In this case he was asking to go via the switchboard, and why wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So according to you, it's Panorama 03 who is located in Panorama who is calling the operator in Panorama?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Are you sure this operator was not located elsewhere? For example, where the person called Rajko was located?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I don't know where he was. I only transcribed what I hear. As for where he was, well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And how did you identify this operator as being the operator of the Panorama location?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: If you are doing things for quite a long time, you recognise people. Just before we started recording, I think he introduced himself. There was a mention of the Panorama switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that when you realised that there was a mistake on line 4, line 4 of the handwritten version, which is underlined, that you spoke to the person who had typed this conversation and that you corrected this mistake.

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Who corrected this mistake? You or the person who typed the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I made the correction, because the typist wasn't allowed to make any corrections. He was supposed to type what was taken down in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What you're saying, I do understand, but the problem is that you only underlined, you did not make any corrections following that, and for example cross out 03 and putting R instead or crossing out R and putting 03 instead. How could possibly the operator know exactly what this line refers to, what you wrote on line 4?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Well, the operator was in the room adjacent to mine. It sufficed that I tell him where the error was, and then I didn't need to make a correction because he would.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And how did you understand that there was a mistake in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Further on in the conversation. We have the time and the names, and then you realise there was a mistake, that you've mixed up the initials. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And do you know why, why the person who typed this conversation did not put down 03 for Panorama 03 or P, and rather wrote down X instead?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I think it was entered so as to make typing easier. Otherwise you would have had two Ps and it would be difficult to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But, sir, in the typewritten text there is no P. Indeed there is an X, a C, and an R. Why in this case would it have been difficult to use P or 03 to be absolutely different or to differentiate them?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: First of all, I think they wanted to make sure that Panorama was the switchboard. And as for 03, so as not to put the whole name, Panorama 03, it was easier for him to put an X there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct to say that one -- that normally one writes an X when the person speaking is unknown?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes, when you don't know who the speakers are, we used Xs and Ys.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it possible that the person who was typing X, who typed X preferred to put an X because it wasn't certain that the person who was speaking was Panorama number 3, 03?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No. He was supposed to type the report as it was in the handwriting. It wasn't up to him to decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You just said that the person was typing should exactly type the report as the conversation was in the notebook, and in the notebook there is 03 written and it's an X in the report. Could you explain this?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes. It is an error. But that correction was done with my consent.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Therefore, you were giving your consent. Instead of 03, you accepted an X to be typed?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No. I think I just told you that it was to make it easier for him to type. An X doesn't represent anything to him, because we know who the speaker is, we saw it in the heading at the beginning. We know who the X is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If I understand you rightly, for convenience's sake for the person who was typing for the computer, the report sent to your superior command were -- there where the report was sent was not quite accurate; isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, I object because it's, in fact, speculative to the state of mind and it is not exactly restating what the witness just answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't see -- we don't see it speculative the way you do, Ms. Soljan, so go ahead, answer the question, please. And the question was as follows: "If I understood you correctly, for convenience's sake for the persons who was typing for the computer, the report sent to your superior --" one moment. "The report sent to your superior command were -- there where the report was sent was not quite accurate; isn't it true?" It's being put to you that because of what you have testified, answering the last questions, reports sent to the superior command would not be accurate. What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree with that. I think there must have been -- I think they were supposed to be typed the way they were taken down by hand. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, concerning this specific report and to conclude on this subject, do you agree that the version which was typed is quite different from the handwritten version, starting by the number of the frequency, the time, and finishing with the participants, collocutors, and the order of people who were speaking. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes. I think there is an error in terms of the time and that the speakers' order was reversed at a certain point, their initials. I think this is as far as the changes go, compared to the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And the frequency is also different, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I think the frequency is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you read what is written on your handwritten text?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In that case -- I'm sorry, in that case, I'm sorry, I thought it was 54. You said that you received orders and listened for a certain period apart from the territory and during another period another part of the territory, you were monitoring those. Do you remember when, and I'm asking you when but not a precise date, when you received the order to monitor oriental [as interpreted] Bosnia where the Drina Corps was.

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: I cannot recall at what time or on what date exactly. But we worked on it for quite a long time, even before the events there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you listened to conversations coming from Sarajevo Corps, from the Sarajevo front. Did you monitor those?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you monitored those conversations during the fights around Sarajevo in June 1995; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: No. When I said we monitored conversations within the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, I had in mind the part of the territory facing our location, not the other part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And where -- which were these parts which were close to the place where you were, your site?

utterances.speaker: PW-135
utterances.text: They were not close to our location. However, from the place where we were, we followed what we could, what was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau. I take it that there are no questions from the Gvero team. Any questions for the Pandurevic team?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we're finished with your testimony, sir, for which I thank you on behalf of the Tribunal. Our staff will assist you now to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. On behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Documents. Prosecution has kindly provided us with a list of documents that they wish to tender. First of which I suppose are no -- there cannot be any problems, the witness statement and his pseudonym sheet. So they are being admitted under seal. The rest are all intercepts, and with the usual caveat, I hear no objections in the first place, so they will be marked for identification purposes, pending the resolution of the existing conversations regarding the intercepts on which we will be approaching you by means of an order, either today or tomorrow. I think I have even signed it already. So I am told we need 10 minutes to install the telephone. Wasn't it installed before already?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. It's okay. I mean I am just -- I know that the staff are extremely cooperative. So we need 10 minutes to change the microphone. Sorry, I said telephone before, but -- yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before we stop, it's a witness to be heard according to Article 92 ter. We received the statement today, that's the problem, and this statement does not exist in B/C/S. I know this is not very popular, but I would like this deposition not to continue and request to cross-examine this witness tomorrow so that the witness can take recognisance [as interpreted] of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you for that, Madam Fauveau. Yes, I see you are in competition. Whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. The statement actually does now exist in B/C/S. We had the statement translated while the other witness was testifying. The original statement was actually typed, transcribed today. So we do have it available for counsel's inspection. I know that she has -- at least I believe she has the English version and has had that for -- I think since maybe a little bit after 1.00 or just about 1.30. So we do have the B/C/S version for your inspection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just want to correct this here. It was not for the direct examination, I said I had nothing against a direct examination today, it's only for the...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The statement, just so that you are aware, it is about two pages single-spaced. Also the substance of the statement is essentially contained in proofing note provided to counsel as well. So there is no substantive difference between what is contained in the statement, the B/C/S version, obviously the English version or the proofing note. But I do understand counsel's concern, and I think it's not a problem for her to examine it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking of witness number 176, aren't we? I just want to make sure that we're talking of the same one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, it's the witness who is supposed to just arrive. Another thing, the proofing notes we just received them now. I have just received them 15 minutes ago. And here it is not a statement, is it a statement of one page or two pages? It is a question of Rule 66, which requests the Prosecutor to show us this in a language which the accused understands. I think we should have the time to be able to consult our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will discuss it outside. May I ask a question to the rest of the Defence teams. Could you indicate whether you have discussed amongst yourselves first the partitioning of the time limit, the two hours 40 minutes -- or two hours 20 minutes, or whether you are going to go for the 20 minutes each? And also, if there are, amongst you, who would like not to cross-examine the witness at all? That would help us so it is out. In the meantime, I was going to suggest that instead of breaking now for 10 minutes until they fix the microphone, we could have a full break of 25 minutes, which would give -- or 20 minutes which would give Madam Fauveau the chance to read through it and then if there are really serious concerns you can come back to us and we will deal with your concerns adequately, depending on how serious they are, obviously. All right. So we will have a 25-minute break starting from now. And we'll take it up after that. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please correct eastern Bosnia instead of oriental Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I understand we can start with this witness, correct? So good afternoon to you, sir. I wish to welcome you in this trial, where you are going to give evidence. Before you start your evidence however, you are required to enter a solemn -- make a solemn declaration that you will testify the truth. The text is going to be handed to you by Madam Usher. Please stand up and read it out so that we can hear you and that will be your undertaking with us that you will testify the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Vanderpuye will be asking you a few questions and he will be making reference to a statement that you gave on the 16th of January of this year. And then we will -- after that we will move to the cross- examination. I am hopeful that within a very short time you will be out of this courtroom and after that soon on your way back home. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I would like to have the pseudonym sheet, please, shown to the witness. For the record, it's PO2364.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you please take a look at that and can you tell us without telling us what's on it, whether or not you are the person named on that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-151
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think there's a mistake about witness P151 and it's not the right number which is given. On line 1, page 50, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness PW-151. Thank you for pointing that out. And the important thing is that it is corrected. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you a few questions. Please try to keep your voice up so that the interpreter can hear you, and try to allow a small pause between question and answer so that everyone can keep up. Did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor signed and dated 17th January 2007?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-151
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Vanderpuye. Is it 17th or 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's actually signed and dated the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. I just wondered because in the list of documents you intend to use, yeah, that's correct. But it's indicated as the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all right. I just make things clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We're talking about the same document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was the statement that you gave at that time a truthful one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-151
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to have your statement read to you before coming to testify today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-151
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that done in your native language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-151
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what language is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-151
utterances.text: Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does the statement as read to you fairly and accurately reflect your declaration or what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-151
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does your -- does the statement fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-151
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At this time I would move to have the statement admitted in evidence under 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I read a brief summary of the statement? I'm sorry, for the record it's PO2363.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness completed electro-technical high school in 1990 and was soon thereafter called upon to complete his compulsory military obligation with the JNA. May I go into private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In 1993, the witness was assigned to the southern site of the Anti-Electronic Warfare Unit, PEB, as an intercept operator. Upon his arrival to the PEB, the witness received instructions concerning the operate of the equipment and began processing intercepted communications in conformity with an established procedure, which entailed taping intercepted communications and manually transcribing them into notebooks. The witness remained in the ABiH or the army, I should say, of Bosnia and Herzegovina until he was demobilised in 1997. That concludes my 92 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just have a few questions I'd like to put to the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us in 1995 what your position was in the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-151
utterances.text: I was a soldier and an operator operating the equipment at the location that was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
